title: If Orban wins, Putin will be delighted
snippet: Foreign interference from Russia in the Hungarian elections is deeply troubling.

Log in or Subscribe Copy link X Icon twitter Facebook Icon facebook WhatsApp Icon whatsapp email Add us as preferred source Copy link X Icon twitter Facebook Icon facebook WhatsApp Icon whatsapp email Orban has pushed Hungary closer to Russia’s orbit Credit: Alexander Nemenov/Reuters Ivana Stradner Published 12 April 2026 2:15pm BST In June 1989, a 26-year-old Viktor Orban demanded free elections and the withdrawal of Soviet troops in what was a defining moment in Hungary’s democratic awakening. He was a young dissident challenging Moscow, a symbol of hope for a country emerging from decades of authoritarian rule.Fast forward to 2026, and the narrative has shifted dramatically. As Hungary approaches the results of its parliamentary elections today, Orban, who once said “Nyet” to Moscow, now cultivates ties with Vladimir Putin and has transformed Hungary into a gateway for foreign meddling.What prompted Orban’s dramatic trajectory from outspoken dissident to Putin puppet? For the first few decades of his political career, Orban was no ally of Russia. During his first time in office, he ushered Hungary into Nato, which constituted an open affront to Putin. It was only upon regaining power in 2010 that Orban abruptly changed his tune on Russia. A placard depicting Viktor Orban and Vladimir Putin as a matryoshka doll is displayed during a protest against the Hungarian leader in Budapest on April 10 Credit: Bernadett Szabo/Reuters He became convinced, in part due to the 2008 financial crisis, that the West was in great decline, and that Hungary’s future depended on carving out a new economic space in Central and Eastern Europe. This meant opening up diplomatically and economically to the East. At the same time, domestic reforms intended to consolidate his hold on power encouraged Orban to move closer to Russia.Energy remains Moscow’s most immediate lever of influence in Budapest, with Orban emphasising how “the foundation of Hungary’s energy security has been and continues to be Russian energy supplies”.Hungary remains one of the last European importers of Russian crude, through the Druzhba Pipeline running through Ukraine. In February, Russia’s Rosatom began construction of Hungary’s Paks II nuclear power project.Moreover, as Orban’s Hungary has become friendlier with Russia, it has become dramatically more authoritarian. Almost immediately after returning to power in 2010 with a supermajority, his party Fidesz rewrote the constitution. Laws impacting the media and NGOs are troubling, and Hungary has passed its own version of the “foreign agent” law.Like Putin, Orban presents himself as a champion of “traditional values” and Christian civilisation, and portraying Hungary as a bulwark against liberal Western culture. Yet, in fact, Hungary has low religious observance, which suggests that his messaging is more political than spiritual. By maintaining a balancing act between Western Europe and Moscow, Orban is able to play each off the other.Why would the Kremlin support Orban? Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Europe has sought to isolate Moscow politically and economically. Hungary, however, has maintained economic and political ties with Russia while obstructing EU support for Ukraine. Hungary has maintained economic and political ties with Russia in the wake of the Ukraine war Credit: VALERY SHARIFULIN/AFP For years, Budapest has repeatedly slowed EU sanctions against Russia, and Orban has made animosity toward Ukraine the centre of his re-election campaign. With some polls now showing Orban’s Fidesz party trailing behind Peter Magyar’s Tisza, it seems Orban has also been turning to Moscow for help clinging to power.Last October, he reportedly told Putin: “I am at your service.” The Kremlin appeared to be returning that loyalty through influence operations aimed at shaping the election, with Russia’s intelligence operatives reportedly even staging an assassination to rally Orban’s supporters.In a striking echo of Moscow’s tactics, Peter Szijjarto, the Hungarian minister of foreign affairs and trade, accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere in the election.
